name: Retainer and mouthguard cleaning
lead: Retainer and mouthguard cleaning is routine hygiene for removable oral appliances such as orthodontic retainers, sports mouthguards and night guards. People do it to keep the appliance clear, odour-free and free of buildup, which keeps breath fresh and helps protect the teeth and gums that the appliance is meant to preserve, so the smile and the results of orthodontic work stay in good shape.[1][3]

Retainers hold teeth in their corrected positions after orthodontic treatment. Wikipedia describes removable retainers as best cleaned before insertion with a soft toothbrush, non-abrasive toothpaste, mild soap or retainer tablets, notes that hot water can warp them and that they should not be soaked overnight, and says poor cleaning can contribute to decay and gum inflammation. Fixed retainers are harder to clean and can accumulate plaque, so they are cleaned as part of the nightly routine.[3]

Reference material on closely related appliances notes that porous acrylic dentures can harbour bacteria and yeast and cause odour when not cleaned well.[1] Wikipedia's mouthguard article describes occlusal splints as typically made of heat-cured acrylic or softer materials.[2] No studies specific to cleaning methods for retainers or mouthguards were identified.

chain: Less plaque, bacterial and yeast buildup and odour
Fresher breath and healthier gums around the teeth
angle.text: A clean retainer or mouthguard avoids odour and plaque transfer into the mouth. People pair cleaning with oral care to keep breath fresh and protect an orthodontic result.

paras: The practice involves regularly cleaning removable appliances that sit in the mouth. Wikipedia lists a Hawley retainer (a wire anchored in an acrylic plate), vacuum-formed clear plastic retainers, and fixed wires bonded behind the front teeth as common types, each with different cleaning needs.[3]

For removable retainers, Wikipedia describes cleaning with a soft toothbrush, non-abrasive toothpaste, mild soap or retainer tablets, and cautions that hot water can warp them and that overnight soaking should be avoided.[3]

The halitosis article identifies unclean acrylic dentures as an intra-oral source of odour because the plastic is porous and lets bacteria and yeast accumulate; it does not address orthodontic retainers or mouthguards specifically.[1]

The mouthguard article reports studies of low compliance with prescribed mouthguard use and describes materials and durability, without covering hygiene.[2] The retainer article reports that fixed retainers can cause plaque buildup and gum inflammation when poorly cleaned.[3]

card.summary: Routine cleaning of retainers and mouthguards to limit bacterial buildup and odour; plausible by analogy to dentures, but little direct study.
card.note: Sources found cover related appliances (dentures), not retainers directly.

quick.overview:
Cleaning retainers and mouthguards is a hygiene habit meant to prevent bacterial buildup and odour.

Reference sources describe bacteria and yeast building up on porous acrylic dentures, a related appliance, but no studies specific to retainers or mouthguards were found.
quick.mechanism: Appliances worn in the mouth can collect biofilm on their surfaces; cleaning removes it. Porous plastic is described as especially able to hold microbes.
quick.risks: No harms from cleaning are reported in the sources consulted. Manufacturers and dentists give product-specific care guidance.
